Pursuant to notice, a hearing was held and the record was closed in Salem,
Oregon on August 1, 2007 before Administrative Law Judge Brazeau. OR-OSHA
was represented by Jeff Dover, Assistant Attorney General. Defendant, Arty’s
A&S Construction, appeared through Artimon Kuzmin, President of the company.
Exhibits 1 through 19 were admitted into evidence in WCB Case. No. SH-
06418. Exhibits 1 through 14 were admitted in WCB Case No. SH-06466.
ISSUES
1. Whether Plaintiff’s Citations and Notifications of penalty should be
“dismissed” on various grounds;
2. Defendant appeals the Citations and Notification of Penalty dated May 9,
2006 and September 15, 2006, arguing that no violations of any pertinent safety
regulation occurred in either case.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Between April 4 and April 12, 2006, Safety Compliance Officer (SCO) Tim
Nelson and SCO Jeff Weaver conducted a comprehensive inspection at
OPINION AND ORDER, Page 1 of 5
KUZMAN/RB/sa/SH06418

Defendant’s construction site in Gervais, Oregon. As they approached the
construction site, the SCO’s noted a worker on a roof, more than 10 feet off the
ground, not wearing or utilizing fall protection. Further inspection revealed that
workers were working without protective helmets in areas in which there was the
potential for objects falling on their heads. A faulty stepladder was in use and
workers were using the top of the ladder as a step. Five employees were using nail
guns without eye and face protective equipment. Employees were also working
without fall protection on, at, above and/or near wall and window openings where
the bottom edge of the wall opening was more than six feet above lower levels and
the inside bottom edge of the wall opening was less than 39 inches above the
working surface. Stairways having four or more risers or rising more than 30
inches were not equipped with handrail and stair rail systems along unprotected
edges. An extension cord in use with a Skilsaw was deformed. Finally, workers
were using a six-foot ladder that had a 2 X 4-inch block of wood attached to its
fiberglass frame with nails.
After interviewing Nicanor Lopez, who advised that he was the construction
foreman, the SCO’s determined that the employer had committed safety violations
involving all of the aforementioned incidents. Because the employer had
previously been cited for fall protection violations, the SCO’s concluded that April,
2006 fall protection violations should be classified as “repeat” violations. The
SCO’s also calculated that some of the current violations were “serious,” while
others were less than serious and in the “other” category. Based on the SCO’s
investigations, as Citation and Notification of Penalty issued on September 15,
2006, citing Defendant for nine alleged violations.
On August 15, 2006, SCO Tim Marcum was traveling in Oregon City,
Oregon when he observed a worker walking the top plate of a two-story residential
building that was under construction. Believing that the worker was in imminent
danger of serious injury from a possible fall, SCO Marcum stopped and conducted
an opening interview with the at-risk employee, Nicanor Lopez, Defendant’s
supervisor on the Gervais, Oregon work site that was the subject of OR-OSHA’s
April, 2006 inspection. After concluding that a fall protection violation had
occurred, Marcum recommended that the employer be cited for a violation of 29
CFR 1926.502(a)(2).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW AND OPINION
1. The employer’s Motion to Dismiss
OPINION AND ORDER, Page 2 of 5
KUZMAN/RB/sa/SH06418

At hearing, the employer provided the forum with a “Motion for Summary
Ruling to Dismiss,” listing three bases for a summary vacating of the Citations
issued in this matter. The first basis listed is that the employer “did not commit”
the violations. That, of course, is the subject of the evidentiary hearing and a
decision that I must make having heard and considered all of the evidence.
Therefore, the employer’s first basis for vacating the Citations cannot be granted.
The second basis listed by the employer suggests that the employer was
“unable” to commit a violation in “February.” Because the violations that are
subject to this proceeding allegedly occurred in April and August, 2006, I am
unsure to what the employer refers. In any event, whether the employer was
“capable” of committing violations is a matter to determined by the evidence
generated at hearing. Therefore, the employer’s second basis for vacating the
Citations cannot be granted.
The third basis listed by the employer is that the fines issued by OR-OSHA
were not “reasonable and justified within Constitutional limits.” The employer has
offered no supporting argument or evidence regarding an alleged violation of the
Constitution and I am, therefore, unable to determine the specific challenge the
employer makes in that regard. As to whether the fines were “reasonable,” I will
refer to the pertinent administrative rules in that regard and determine whether the
fines were appropriate under the applicable standards.
The employer’s Motion to Dismiss is denied.
2. The merits of the Citations
After the completion of OR-OSHA’s case in chief at hearing, Mr. Kuzmin,
the employer, testified. During his testimony, he effectively conceded that the
violations alleged by OR-OSHA had occurred. He also, however, offered evidence
that while he provided safety equipment to his employees, he was unable to ensure
their proper use of it because of his being unable to be in more than one of his
construction sites at a time. I interpreted Mr. Kuzmin’s explanation to be an
assertion of the “rogue supervisor/rogue employees” defense.
A showing by the employer that it has an adequate and effectively enforced
safety program, gives rise to the inference that the employer's reliance on
employees to comply with applicable safety rules is justifiable; violations then are
not foreseeable or preventable. On the other hand, common sense and experience
suggest that an employer who has not implemented an effective safety program
OPINION AND ORDER, Page 3 of 5
KUZMAN/RB/sa/SH06418

should know employees are likely to violate rules designed to guard against
foreseeable risks attendant to that employer's business. See Danco Const. Co. v.
OSHRC, 586 F.2d 1243 (8th Cir. 1978); Mountain States Tel. And Tel. V.
Occupational Safety, 623 F.2d 155 (10th Cir. 1980). (describing rationale
underlying rogue supervisor defense).
In OR-OSHA v. Don Whitaker Logging, 148 Or App 464 (1997), the court
held that when a supervisor commits a violation, pertinent administrative rules do
not require that the supervisor's knowledge of that violation be imputed to the
employer. The Supreme Court reversed the court’s decision, however, in OR-
OSHA v. Don Whitaker Logging, 329 Or 256 (1999), holding that in general,
OR-OSHA has the burden of proving that: (1) a supervisor personally committed a
serious violation of a safety law; and (2) the supervisor was acting within the scope
of his authorized duties. If OR-OSHA proves those elements, facts that the
supervisor knew or reasonably could have known are attributable to employer
because of their agency relationship. On the other hand, an employer is not
responsible for a safety violation if it "did not, and could not with the exercise of
reasonable diligence, know of the presence of the violation." OAR 437-001-
0015(62)(a)(A). If OR-OSHA presents evidence demonstrating employer's
knowledge under OAR 437-001-0760(3)(c), employer still may offer relevant
evidence that, in the particular circumstances, it should not be held responsible.
Thus, the question in the present case is whether the employer has presented
sufficient evidence that he did not, and could not have known of the violations
committed by his supervisor (after exercising reasonable diligence). After
carefully reviewing the record, I conclude that the employer has failed to provide
sufficient evidence to support his defense. Two facts tend to refute his assertion.
First, that the employer has been cited on prior occasions for the same violation
committed by his supervisor in the Citations at issue establishes that he had actual
knowledge of the type and extent of the potential violations. Because of that
knowledge, I find that the employer should have been acutely concerned about
repeat violations and should have taken extraordinary steps to ensure they did not
occur. Here, there is evidence that the employer provided safety equipment to
employees, but there is also evidence that the equipment may have been
inadequate, both in terms of quality and quantity.
Perhaps more important, the supervisor subject to the two 2006 fall
protection violations was the same supervisor employed by Defendant in 2004,
when the employer was first cited for similar fall protection violations. While the
employer may have provided training, and perhaps have even sanctioned, Lopez
OPINION AND ORDER, Page 4 of 5
KUZMAN/RB/sa/SH06418

for the prior violations, he did not terminate Lopez’s employment or take other
extraordinary steps to ensure that repeat violations would not occur. That Lopez
was involved once again in the violations committed on two occasions in 2006
suggests that the employer failed to adequately enforce whatever safety provisions
he may have put in place.
I conclude that OR-OSHA’s Citations were properly issued and that the
classification and amount of penalties (which the employer has not specifically
contested) were consistent with the pertinent administrative rules.
ORDER
Plaintiff’s Citations and Notifications of Penalty dated May 9, 2006 and
September 15, 2006 are affirmed as written.
NOTICE TO ALL PARTIES: You are entitled to judicial review of this
Order. Proceedings for review are to be instituted by filing a petition in the Court
of Appeals, Supreme Court Building, Salem, Oregon 97301-2563, within 60 days
following the date this Order is entered and served as shown hereon. The
procedure for such judicial review is prescribed by ORS 183.480 and ORS
183.482.
Entered at Portland, Oregon on August 20, 2007.
Workers' Compensation Board
Robert Brazeau
Administrative Law Judge
